clue.text: However old the oil, it's of aviation body

definitions.text: However old the oil, it's of aviation body

parts.words: However old the oil, it's of aviation body
parts.note: whatever the age of the oil, it is the fuel's age, and run together those words come within a letter-swap of the main body of an aeroplane

explanation.surface: A remark that, whatever the age of the lubricant, it belongs to the aircraft industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil' stands for fuel: the phrase 'the fuel's age' is played on, with its S moved, to give the aircraft's body.
explanation.definitionFit: The central hull of an aeroplane, to which wings and tail attach, is its main body.

clue.text: A habitual overtaker

parts.note: not a driver passing cars, but someone whose job is to take people over, across water

explanation.surface: A motorist who constantly passes other cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overtaker' suggests passing on the road; read as 'one who takes over', it is the boatman carrying passengers across a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A boatman who carries passengers across a river daily takes them over as his trade.

clue.text: Write-it-yourself tune ?

parts.note: the thing one writes oneself is one's name, and a programme's theme music is called by the same word plus tune

explanation.surface: A do-it-yourself melody kit for amateur songwriters.
explanation.walkthrough: A signature tune is a theme for a show or performer; a signature is the one thing you must write yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: One's handwritten name is written only by oneself, and a performer's theme is a signature tune.

clue.text: Sits back, look, by going fifty-fifty with Bob

parts.note: lo is an old word for look
L is the Roman numeral fifty, twice
a bob was a shilling, abbreviated s in old British money

explanation.surface: Someone relaxes, sharing equally with a friend called Bob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifty-fifty' sounds like an equal share; it is two Roman fifties, LL. A bob was slang for a shilling, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: To loll is to lounge or recline lazily, sitting back.

clue.text: Gun once got on the heather ?

parts.note: gat is an archaic past tense of get, as in the Bible
ling is the common heather

explanation.surface: A firearm was once carried onto the moor.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts GAT above LING. The Gatling was a hand-cranked machine gun of the nineteenth century, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gatling was an early rapid-fire weapon, now obsolete.

clue.text: Mine author

parts.note: the maker or author of a mine is a military tunneller who digs it, and that title was also the pen-name of a thriller writer

explanation.surface: A writer whose book belongs to the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Sapper was the pen-name of H. C. McNeile, creator of Bulldog Drummond; a sapper is also a soldier who digs mines.
explanation.definitionFit: A military engineer digging tunnels under enemy works authored mines, and the Bulldog Drummond novelist wrote under that name.

clue.text: Following singular work with figures there is further growth

parts.note: after means following
math, singular, is mathematics

explanation.surface: After doing sums alone, there is more development.
explanation.walkthrough: An aftermath is literally a second mowing: the grass that grows after the first crop is cut.
explanation.definitionFit: The old farming sense is a second crop of grass, regrowth after the first harvest.

clue.text: Supplanting teddy-bear and embraced by the older generation

indicators.note: embraced by means the word and sits inside the letters for the older generation

parts.note: pa, father, is of the older generation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A new toy bear replaces the teddy and is loved by grandparents.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1930s and 40s the giant panda became a popular soft toy, displacing the teddy bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Toy versions of the black-and-white bear became a fashion that rivalled the teddy.

clue.text: Peary's returns

annotationWithheld.why: Peary's returns (6): REPAYS is an anagram of PEARYS, but 'returns' must be both the definition and the anagram indicator, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Work for woman with iron-or man of course ?

definitions.meaning: to crimp or flute frills with a heated iron, once a laundress's job
a man on the golf course, with golf said in the old way as 'goff'

explanation.definitionFit: Goffering is pleating linen with a hot iron; and in old genteel speech golf rhymed with off, making its player a 'goffer'.

clue.text: Latvian's get-up is nothing if not operatic

definitions.note: an adjective for a noun answer: the clue means the answer is nothing if not an opera

parts.note: a get-up is an outfit, a rig
nothing is zero, the letter O
a Lett is a Latvian
'not' sounds like nought, a zero, so the letter O

explanation.surface: A Baltic man's outfit is extravagantly theatrical.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in answer order RIG, O, LETT, O, not the clue's order. Rigoletto is Verdi's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's work about a court jester is an opera through and through, so the clue calls it operatic.

clue.text: Quite a load for such a speed

definitions.text: Quite a load for such a speed

parts.words: Quite a load for such a speed
parts.note: a hundredweight-style load of a ton, and the motorcyclist's slang for doing a hundred miles an hour

explanation.surface: A remark that a vehicle is carrying a heavy load to be going so fast.
explanation.walkthrough: A ton is quite a load; 'the ton' is also slang for a hundred miles an hour, and doing it is going ton-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Ton-up describes travelling at a hundred miles per hour, the 'ton' being the slang hundred.

clue.text: Yes, the best man turned poet

parts.note: yea is an old word for yes

indicators.note: turned means the letters for the best man are read in reverse

parts.note: a saint, ST, is the best of men

explanation.surface: Agreement that the groom's attendant has become a writer of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best man' suggests a wedding, but a saint is the best of men; 'turned' reverses his abbreviation. W. B. Yeats was the Irish poet.
explanation.definitionFit: W. B. Yeats was the Irish Nobel laureate in literature, famous for his verse.

clue.text: Hospital for a contrary tree-sitter

parts.note: one sitting up a tree is in a fir
'Mary, Mary, quite contrary' is the nursery rhyme

explanation.surface: A ward for an awkward person perched in a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary' makes 'a contrary' MARY; whoever sits in a tree is IN FIR.
explanation.definitionFit: An infirmary is an old name for a hospital caring for the sick.

clue.text: Slinging mud at a vehicle in the Greek capital

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle
taken as written

indicators.note: the capital, or first letter, of the word Greek is taken

explanation.surface: Throwing dirt at a coach in Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Greek capital' looks like Athens, but it is the capital letter of 'Greek', G.
explanation.definitionFit: Slinging mud is hurling insults, which is verbally attacking someone.

clue.text: Where 12 had beans without apparently needing one

definitions.text: Where 12 had beans without apparently needing one

parts.words: Where 12 had beans without apparently needing one
parts.note: 12 is the poet, who planned nine bean-rows on a lake isle; the place's name read as a phrase says a hostelry costs nothing

explanation.surface: Where a poet grew beans, seemingly without needing a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats wrote 'Nine bean-rows will I have there' in The Lake Isle of Innisfree; the name splits as INN IS FREE, so one needn't buy an inn.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish lake island is where the poet imagined a cabin and his bean-rows.

clue.text: .Make friends again, d'you mean it ?

definitions.meaning: to ally once more, to renew a friendship
an exclamation of surprise asking whether something is true

explanation.definitionFit: Re-ally is to form an alliance anew; and the single-word question of surprise asks 'is that so?'

clue.text: Dear fruit ?

parts.note: love is a term of endearment, like dear
an apple is a fruit

explanation.surface: An expensive piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' suggests expensive; it is the endearment LOVE. Love apple is an old name for the tomato.
explanation.definitionFit: Love apple is an old name for the tomato, so the whole clue is a fruit of love.

clue.text: One so boozes as to be atomic !

definitions.note: an adjective for a noun answer: the things are atomic variants

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written
to tope is to drink heavily

explanation.surface: Someone drinks so much as to be blown away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Atomic' looks like slang for very drunk; it defines atoms of one element with differing neutrons.
explanation.definitionFit: These are forms of a chemical element differing in atomic mass, a matter of atomic structure.

clue.text: It's character-forming, that's the point

parts.note: character here means a written letter, and the thing that forms letters is a sharp metal tip

explanation.surface: A claim that some hardship builds moral fibre, which is its purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character-forming' sounds like moral improvement; here characters are handwritten letters, formed by the point of a writing instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal tip of a dip or fountain pen forms letters on the page and is literally a point.

clue.text: Game that puts 1 down out of a job

definitions.meaning: a card game for four players in pairs

definitions.text: that puts 1 down out of a job
definitions.meaning: a river crossing built over the water makes the boatman at 1 down redundant

explanation.definitionFit: Contract is a card game of that name; and a span over a river ends the need for a boat crossing.

clue.text: Acts so as to be with those that are better off

parts.note: taken as written
the haves are the well-off, as in haves and have-nots

explanation.surface: Someone performs in order to mix with the rich.
explanation.definitionFit: To behave is to conduct oneself, and so to act in a given way.

clue.text: Look in your bank-book and see stars !

definitions.text: Look in your bank-book and see stars

parts.words: Look in your bank-book and see stars
parts.note: a bank-book shows what is left in the account, and among the stars is Libra, the scales

explanation.surface: Check your savings and be dazzled.
explanation.walkthrough: A bank-book shows your balance; Libra, the scales or Balance, is a constellation and zodiac sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The sum left in an account is its balance, and the zodiac's scales are called the Balance.

clue.text: Pub art, make it snappy

indicators.note: make it tells the solver to make something new from the letters of pub art

explanation.surface: A pub painting done in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make it snappy' reads as 'hurry up'; 'make it' is the signal to rearrange PUBART.
explanation.definitionFit: Snappy, as in curt or short, means brusque and sudden.

clue.text: Home of the eminent Tusker, Oxon.

definitions.text: Home of the eminent Tusker, Oxon.

parts.words: Home of the eminent Tusker, Oxon.
parts.note: a tusker is a boar, its eminence a hill, and the place so named in Oxfordshire was home to eminent people

explanation.surface: The address of a famous elephant, in Oxfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxon. is the abbreviation for Oxfordshire. Boars Hill, near Oxford, was home to poets such as Robert Bridges and John Masefield.
explanation.definitionFit: Boars Hill is a village on high ground south-west of Oxford, long a home for writers and scholars.

clue.text: A devoted housemaster

parts.note: not a schoolteacher in charge of a boarding house, but the head of a religious house of monks devoted to God

explanation.surface: A dedicated teacher running a boarding house at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housemaster' suggests a public school; here the house is a monastery and devotion is religious.
explanation.definitionFit: The superior of a monastery is master of a religious house.

clue.text: Fright pales the red-headed bird

indicators.note: to pale is to lose redness, so the red is taken out of the bird's name

parts.note: the redstart is a small songbird whose name begins with red

explanation.surface: A scare drains the colour from a bird with a crimson crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red-headed' says the bird's name has RED at its head; 'pales' removes that RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A start is a sudden jump of alarm, a fright.

clue.text: Give promise of profanity

definitions.meaning: to take an oath, to vow
a noun: to use profane language, to curse

explanation.definitionFit: One vows under oath, and one also curses with bad language; the same verb does both.

clue.text: What colour the river, Heep ?

indicators.note: Uriah Heep in Dickens's David Copperfield drops his aitches, calling himself 'umble, so the opening H goes

parts.note: the Humber is an English river estuary

explanation.surface: Someone asks Uriah Heep the colour of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep, from Dickens, says ''umble' for humble; spoken his way, the Humber loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Umber is a brown earth pigment, and the name of that colour.

clue.text: Hot stuff, dad, when bottled!

parts.note: ginger is a hot spice
pop is a name for father

explanation.surface: Something fiery for father, once it is in a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a fizzy drink flavoured with hot ginger, sold bottled.
explanation.definitionFit: Ginger pop is a bottled fizzy drink flavoured with the spicy root.

clue.text: To get sent back into Devon

definitions.note: the clue's 'into Devon' points to a place in that county, not the county itself

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: sent back means the letters of sent are reversed

explanation.surface: Being told to get dispatched home to the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' makes the word sent read in reverse. Totnes is a market town in Devon, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Totnes is a historic market town on the River Dart in the county.

clue.text: House empty? Don't be so myopic!

definitions.meaning: the House of Lords with its peers gone
the short-sighted squint, so the advice is to squint less

explanation.definitionFit: A Lords chamber without lords would be without a peer; and someone short-sighted is told to stop squinting so much; the word means unrivalled.
